title: Made to Stick: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die
author: Chip Heath and Dan Heath
thesis: Ideas become understandable, memorable, and capable of changing thought or behavior when communicators deliberately build six qualities into them: simplicity, unexpectedness, concreteness, credibility, emotion, and story. The recurring obstacle is expert knowledge that makes the communicator forget what an uninitiated audience does not yet know.
teachingArc: The introduction defines stickiness and the curse of knowledge, then the six numbered units develop the SUCCESs checklist one quality at a time. The sequence moves from selecting a compact core and opening a knowledge gap, through giving the idea sensory form and self-contained proof, to making the stakes personally meaningful and packaging action inside narrative. An epilogue recombines the qualities as a diagnostic path from attention to action rather than adding a seventh authored unit.

signatureMoves: opens an idea with a surprising named case before extracting the communication principle
pairs memorable labels with operational distinctions and short diagnostic questions
uses contrasting message versions and clinic-style rewrites to expose why one formulation travels
moves between business, education, public health, military, and popular-culture settings
returns to the curse of knowledge as the practical antagonist behind expert communication failures
avoidMoves: does not rely on abstract theory without a concrete case
does not treat brevity alone as sufficient for simplicity
does not present the six qualities as a rigid step-by-step formula
